Our tool is an adverse-event capture and reporting app for hospital pharmacists and nurses: when a patient has a suspected reaction to a drug, staff log it on the ward, the app structures it, and it's supposed to route the report onward to the manufacturer and the national authority. I'm the regulatory affairs lead and, frankly, fairly confident we've got the compliance bones right — but tell me where the holes are.

It's a good sign you're confident on the bones — let me probe the parts of pharmacovigilance tooling that tend to fail quietly rather than loudly. Let me start with the routing, since that's the whole point of the tool.

Two questions: (1) When a report is logged on the ward, what guarantees it actually *reaches* the manufacturer and the national competent authority — is the onward transmission confirmed and tracked, or fire-and-forget? (2) For serious adverse events, do you enforce the regulatory reporting timelines, or is timing left to the staff and downstream process?

Honestly the onward routing is the weakest part. We capture and structure the report well, but transmission to the authority is a nightly batch that sometimes fails silently, and we don't track delivery confirmation per report. And no, we don't enforce the serious-case clock — we assume the safety team handles deadlines.

That's the hole, and it's a significant one because the purpose of the tool is the reporting, not the capturing.

**[P7.D5] Post-Market Surveillance & Vigilance** — Pharmacovigilance reporting exists so that safety signals reach manufacturers and authorities in time to act. A nightly batch that can fail silently with no per-report delivery confirmation means adverse events can be logged on the ward, look 'reported' to staff, and never actually arrive — the signal dies in your pipe. For *serious* cases there are hard regulatory clocks (under EU pharmacovigilance, serious adverse reactions to medicines are expedited — 15-day reporting; the device-side equivalent under MDR 2017/745 vigilance has its own short deadlines for serious incidents). If your tool neither guarantees delivery nor enforces the clock, it can cause a missed or late mandatory report — a compliance failure with direct patient-safety consequences.

Mitigation: make transmission reliable and acknowledged — per-report delivery confirmation/acknowledgement from the receiving system, automatic retry, and a visible 'undelivered/failed' state that escalates rather than fails silently; track each report's status end-to-end. Triage seriousness at capture and drive the relevant expedited clock with reminders/escalation so a serious case can't sit unsent.

This ties straight to your documentation obligations:

**[P7.D7] Lifecycle & Documentation Management** — A reporting tool needs a defensible, durable record of each report's full lifecycle: created, edited, transmitted, acknowledged, by whom, when, and which version of the report. If you can't reconstruct that audit trail, you can't demonstrate compliance, can't investigate a missed report, and can't satisfy an inspection.

What does your audit trail and versioning look like today — and what happens to a report that's edited after initial submission?

We keep the final report, but edits overwrite in place — we don't version, so if someone amends a report after submission we lose the original and there's no clear trail of who changed what. The audit log is thin. I can see that's a problem for an inspection.

It is, and overwrite-in-place is the specific anti-pattern to fix.

**[P7.D7] (continued) Lifecycle & Documentation Management** — In-place overwrite destroys the evidentiary chain. Pharmacovigilance and quality-management expectations (and good documentation practice generally) require that you can show what was reported, when, by whom, and what every subsequent amendment changed — follow-up reports should supplement, not silently replace, the original. You also need traceable versioning of the *tool itself* (a defined SOP, change control, validated releases) since the software is part of a regulated safety process.

Mitigation: immutable, append-only report records with full versioning and a complete who/what/when audit log; treat amendments as new versions linked to the original; document the system under change control with SOPs. ISO 82304-2 and your QMS expect this lifecycle documentation.

Now let me check the clinical-content side, because a structured AE tool makes interpretive claims:

**[P5.D3] Decision Traceability & Logging** — When the app 'structures' a report — coding the suspected drug, the reaction, seriousness, causality — those are interpretive steps. If staff can't see and the record can't show how a free-text ward note became a coded, seriousness-classified report (and who confirmed it), you lose traceability of the very classification that drives the reporting clock. A miscoded 'non-serious' that was actually serious is how a deadline gets missed invisibly.

How is the structuring done — manual coding by staff, or does the app auto-suggest the drug/reaction/seriousness coding?

It auto-suggests the coding and seriousness from the free text, and staff usually just accept it — they're busy. We don't record whether they reviewed the suggestion or whether the seriousness was auto-set or human-confirmed. And there's no patient consent or privacy framing around the report data, which now that you mention it includes patient details.

Two more risks, then — one on the coding, one on the data.

**[P5.D3] (continued) Decision Traceability & Logging** — Auto-suggested seriousness that staff rubber-stamp under time pressure, with no record of whether a human reviewed or the value was auto-set, means your most safety-critical field (seriousness drives the reporting clock) is being decided by an algorithm invisibly. Log, per field, whether the value was auto-suggested and whether a human confirmed it, and require explicit confirmation for the seriousness classification. (This is also an automation-bias-adjacent failure: busy staff defer to the suggestion — so make the seriousness call a deliberate, recorded human step.)

**[P2.D3] Storage, Encryption & Security** — Adverse-event reports contain identifiable patient health data (the affected patient, the drug, the reaction) — special-category data under **GDPR Art. 9** — plus reporter identity. This sits on ward devices and moves across a transmission pipeline. It needs encryption at rest and in transit, strong access control, and a clear, documented lawful basis and retention policy. Pharmacovigilance reporting generally has a legal-obligation basis, which helps, but that doesn't remove the security, minimisation, and transparency duties — and patients/reporters should be informed how the data is handled. Run a DPIA given special-category data at scale in a safety-critical flow.

Mitigation: encrypt at rest and in transit, role-based access, documented lawful basis (legal obligation for the mandatory report) and retention, transparency to data subjects, and a DPIA. Minimise to what the report actually requires.

Let me consolidate the holes you asked for.

**Pharmacovigilance reporter — HERA risk summary**
- [P7.D5] Silent-failing nightly batch with no delivery confirmation, and no enforcement of the serious-case clock — reliable acknowledged transmission with retry and escalating failure states, per-report end-to-end status, and seriousness-driven expedited timelines (EU PV 15-day expedited; MDR 2017/745 vigilance deadlines).
- [P7.D7] In-place overwrite destroys the audit chain — immutable append-only versioned records, full who/what/when log, amendments as linked versions, tool under change control/SOPs (ISO 82304-2).
- [P5.D3] Auto-suggested coding/seriousness rubber-stamped invisibly — record auto-vs-human per field, require explicit human confirmation of seriousness, expose how free text became the coded report.
- [P2.D3] Identifiable patient + reporter data on ward devices and in transit with no privacy framing — encryption at rest/in transit, RBAC, documented lawful basis (legal obligation) and retention, transparency, DPIA (GDPR Art. 9).

The one-line message: your strong capture front-end is hiding a weak, silent reporting back-end — the [P7.D5] guaranteed-delivery-and-clock problem is the one that can cause a missed mandatory report, so fix that and the [P7.D7] audit trail first.

Let me walk you through our care-home monitoring platform: sensors in residents' rooms — bed pressure mats, door sensors, a low-res ceiling camera with on-device 'activity' detection — feed a staff dashboard so carers get alerted to falls, wandering at night, or unusual inactivity. I'm the clinical lead for the home group. My instinct is this is mostly upside for resident safety, but I want the ethical risks named clearly.

It can be real upside — and care-home monitoring is also one of the sharpest autonomy-and-dignity contexts in this whole space, so let me name those clearly rather than only the technical risks. Let me start with who is actually deciding to be monitored.

Two questions: (1) The residents — how many have dementia or otherwise reduced capacity, and who consents to the monitoring: the resident, a relative, or the home? (2) Can a resident who doesn't want a camera or sensors in their room decline it, or is monitoring applied as a blanket default across the home?

A large share have dementia. Consent is basically the home's admission paperwork that the family signs, and monitoring is on by default in every room — we hadn't really framed it as something a resident opts into or out of. It just comes with the placement.

That's the heart of the ethical risk, and it's two distinct dimensions stacked.

**[P2.D6] Vulnerable Population Data** — You're continuously capturing intimate behavioural data — movement, presence, night-time activity, camera-derived activity — about elderly residents, many with dementia, in the place they live, with consent provided by the home's admission paperwork and a family signature. That is high-risk processing of a vulnerable population's special-category data (**GDPR Art. 9**), and 'it comes with the placement' is not a valid consent model for the resident. Where a resident lacks capacity you need a lawful, ethical substitute-decision process — not a blanket admission checkbox. A ceiling camera in someone's bedroom is especially sensitive (private moments, intimate care, undressing).

Mitigation: build a capacity-aware framework — assess and involve the resident to the extent they can participate, use documented proxy/best-interests decisions where they can't, and revisit it (capacity and preferences change). Run a DPIA: vulnerable subjects + continuous behavioural/visual monitoring squarely triggers GDPR Art. 35. Minimise the most intrusive sensing (does every room need a camera, or only those with a specific assessed fall risk?).

Which connects directly to autonomy:

**[P3.D1] Right to Make Decisions** — Blanket, default-on monitoring with no opt-out overrides the resident's right to decide how they're observed in their own home. A resident with capacity who'd rather not have a camera should be able to refuse it; a resident with fluctuating capacity should have their expressed wishes and dignity treated as first-class, not overridden for the home's convenience. Surveillance imposed for safety can quietly erode the autonomy and dignity that the placement is supposed to protect.

Mitigation: make monitoring genuinely opt-in/opt-out at the resident level where capacity allows, offer least-intrusive options (e.g. pressure mat or door sensor instead of camera), and document a dignity-centred rationale per resident rather than a blanket default.

Now the safety mechanics — when the system detects a fall or night wandering and alerts staff, how do carers use that alert, and what's your evidence the detection actually works for this population?

Carers increasingly rely on the dashboard — if it's quiet, they assume everyone's fine and do fewer in-person rounds at night. The detection was tuned on general adult movement, not specifically frail dementia residents, and we haven't independently validated it. So 'no alert' is being treated as 'all well.'

That 'no alert = all well' inference, on top of unvalidated detection, is a serious safety risk — and it interacts badly with the autonomy issue.

**[P3.D1] (the over-reliance face of it)** — When carers cut in-person night rounds because the dashboard is quiet, the system has effectively replaced human attention rather than augmenting it. For frail, cognitively impaired residents, a missed event (a quiet slump out of a sensor's view, a deterioration that produces no 'activity' signal) meets a withdrawn safety net — worse than before the system. 'No alert' is not 'all well'; it can equally mean the system didn't see it.

Mitigation: define the dashboard as assistive, not a replacement for human rounds — protect a minimum in-person check protocol regardless of dashboard state, and train staff explicitly that silence is not assurance. Surface system health: if a sensor is offline, occluded, or a camera's view is blocked, that must be visible, not silent.

**[P7.D6] Third-Party Audit & Certification** — You're deploying safety-critical detection that was tuned on general adult movement, never independently validated for frail dementia residents, into a vulnerable population. Self-asserted performance isn't enough here: the detection's real-world sensitivity (and false-alarm burden, which causes alarm fatigue) for *this* population should be independently validated and, where the function meets the threshold, the product assessed for the appropriate conformity/certification. If the system is intended to detect medically significant events to drive care, that pushes it toward medical-device territory under MDR 2017/745, with notified-body involvement; independent audit/certification is how you and the families can trust it does what's claimed.

Mitigation: validate detection on a representative resident population with independent oversight; pursue the relevant third-party conformity assessment/certification rather than relying on internal tuning; report sensitivity and false-alarm rates honestly to the homes.

Last area — what data leaves the room, who can view the camera/feeds and history, and how long is it kept?

The activity detection is on-device, but events plus short video clips get sent to a central dashboard that many staff can access, and we keep clips indefinitely 'in case they're useful.' Families can also get a viewing login. There's no real consent conversation with the resident about any of that.

That last part is where the privacy exposure concentrates, and it loops back to consent.

**[P2.D1] Informed Consent** — Indefinite retention of bedroom video clips, broad staff access, and family viewing logins are each a significant processing purpose that the people affected have never genuinely been informed of or agreed to. Informed consent (or, given capacity issues, a properly documented lawful basis and best-interests process) requires that residents/their representatives understand specifically what's captured, who can see it, family access, and how long it's kept — not a one-line admission clause. Indefinite retention of intimate footage 'in case' is the opposite of data minimisation and purpose limitation.

Mitigation: a clear, capacity-appropriate consent/transparency process covering each purpose (event detection, clip review, family access, retention); strict role-based access (not 'many staff' — least privilege); a defined, short retention period with automatic deletion and a justified exception only for a specific incident under review; and careful thought about whether families should see live/historic bedroom footage at all, given the resident's dignity. This all belongs in the DPIA.

Let me consolidate for your clinical-governance review.

**Care-home monitoring — HERA risk summary**
- [P2.D6] Continuous behavioural/visual monitoring of vulnerable, often dementia residents under admission-paperwork consent — capacity-aware/proxy best-interests framework, minimise intrusive sensing (camera only on assessed need), DPIA (GDPR Art. 9, Art. 35).
- [P3.D1] Blanket default-on monitoring overrides residents' autonomy, and carers cutting night rounds turns it into a withdrawn safety net — resident-level opt-out and least-intrusive options; keep the dashboard assistive with a protected in-person round protocol; 'no alert' is not 'all well'; surface sensor/camera-offline state.
- [P7.D6] Detection tuned on general adults, never validated for frail dementia residents — independent validation on a representative population and appropriate third-party conformity assessment/certification (MDR 2017/745 if it's detecting clinically significant events); report true sensitivity/false-alarm rates.
- [P2.D1] Indefinite bedroom-clip retention, broad staff access, family viewing logins with no consent conversation — informed/transparent consent per purpose, least-privilege access, short defined retention with auto-deletion, reconsider family access to bedroom footage.

The one-line message for governance: the technology's upside is real, but it's being deployed by overriding the autonomy and consent of the most vulnerable residents and on unvalidated detection — fix the [P2.D6]/[P2.D1] consent-and-minimisation basis and protect the human night-round [P3.D1] first, because those are live ethical exposures from day one.

Bringing this to you as the integration architect: we've built a deterioration-risk flagging module that plugs into the hospital EHR. It reads vitals, labs, and nursing observations from the record, computes an early-warning deterioration score, and writes a risk flag back into the patient's chart that clinicians see on the ward. My focus is the integration layer, but I suspect there are risks beyond plumbing.

There are — and several of them actually live *in* the plumbing, which is good news for someone with your focus. Let me start exactly there.

Two questions: (1) When you read vitals, labs, and nursing observations out of the EHR, how do you handle the cases where data is missing, stale, mis-mapped, or arrives late from a different system — does the score still compute and flag? (2) When you write the flag *back* into the chart, what standard/format do you use, and how does a clinician know how fresh the inputs behind that flag are?

If a value is missing the model imputes or uses the last known value, and it still produces a score — there's no 'insufficient/stale data' state. Write-back is via an HL7 interface but the flag in the chart is just a value; it doesn't carry which inputs or what timestamps it was based on. Latency between source systems is honestly variable.

That's the integration risk with clinical teeth, so let me make it concrete.

**[P4.D2] Interoperability & Data Exchange** — Reading from multiple source systems with variable latency, imputing or carrying-forward missing values, and still emitting a confident score means the flag can be computed on stale or incomplete data and the clinician has no way to know. Carried-forward vitals are a classic deterioration-scoring trap: a patient's last-known-good observation masks a current decline, the score looks reassuring, and the flag is silently wrong. Writing back a bare value with no provenance — which inputs, which timestamps, which were imputed — strips the clinician of the context needed to trust or distrust it. Interoperability here isn't just 'does the HL7 message parse'; it's whether the *clinical meaning and freshness* survive the exchange.

Mitigation: define and surface an explicit 'insufficient/stale data — score not reliable' state instead of always producing a number; carry provenance with the flag (input timestamps, which values were imputed/carried-forward, source system); validate the end-to-end mapping (units, reference ranges, identity matching) and handle late/out-of-order messages deterministically. Consider FHIR for richer structured exchange where the EHR supports it. ISO 82304-2 and MDR 2017/745 expect this data-integrity and error-handling for software in the clinical environment.

This feeds straight into what the clinician sees:

**[P5.D1] Understandable Output** — A bare risk value in the chart, with no inputs, no freshness, no drivers, is not understandable output for a deterioration decision. The clinician can't tell whether a high score reflects a genuinely worsening patient or a data artefact (a mis-mapped unit, an imputed value), nor whether a reassuring score is built on stale inputs.

Is the score an interpretable early-warning rule (NEWS-style) or an ML model — and does the flag show what's driving it?

It's an ML model, more complex than NEWS, and no — the flag shows a number and a colour, nothing about drivers. We thought clinicians would prefer a clean single signal rather than clutter. And it was trained on data from the two large teaching hospitals in our group.

The 'clean single signal' instinct is understandable but it's working against you here, and the training-data point raises a separate flag.

**[P5.D1] (continued) Understandable Output** — For an ML deterioration model, a number-and-colour with no drivers forces blind trust and removes the clinician's ability to sanity-check the model against the patient in front of them. Understandable output means surfacing the top contributing factors, the input freshness, and a calibrated sense of how concerning the score is — enough for the clinician to reason, not just react. 'Clean' that hides the reasoning isn't clarity, it's opacity.

Mitigation: show the key drivers and the data freshness alongside the flag, frame it as decision support, and design so a clinician can drill in when it matters.

**[P6.D1] Data & Clinical Rule Bias** — Trained only on two large teaching hospitals in your group, the model has learned those populations and care patterns. Deployed to a different setting (a smaller district hospital, a different demographic mix, different documentation habits for nursing observations), its calibration can drift — under-flagging deterioration in patient groups under-represented in training, or mis-scoring where observation practices differ. Deterioration physiology and its documentation also vary by age, ethnicity, and comorbidity; a narrowly-trained model can systematically miss some groups. That's a direct, differential safety risk.

Mitigation: evaluate calibration and sensitivity per subgroup and per deploying site; validate before going live at any site outside the training distribution; monitor real-world performance by group and site continuously; document the training population's limits. The EU AI Act high-risk regime requires this data-governance and representativeness work, and it's core safety regardless.

Two regulatory items I want to make sure aren't assumed away — has the module's own classification and its data-protection footprint been handled?

Classification — we've leaned on it being 'part of the EHR,' which has its own approvals, so we assumed we inherit that. And on data protection, since the data already lives in the EHR and we're inside the hospital, we figured no new obligations there. Are both of those wrong?

Both are shakier than they sound — let me take each.

On classification: software that computes a deterioration-risk score to drive clinical action is medical-device software in its own right and likely high-risk AI under the EU AI Act (clinical risk-scoring intended to inform care), regardless of being embedded in the EHR — you don't automatically inherit the EHR's regulatory status for a new diagnostic/predictive function. That needs its own conformity assessment under MDR 2017/745 and the AI Act obligations (risk management, human oversight, logging). I'll flag it but the dimension I want to spend the budget on is your data-protection assumption, because that's the one you stated most confidently:

**[P7.D4] GDPR Compliance (DPO/DPIA)** — 'The data's already in the EHR so there are no new obligations' is not correct. You are introducing a *new processing purpose* — automated profiling/risk-scoring of patients — over special-category health data (**GDPR Art. 9**). New purpose, new accountability: this is exactly the kind of large-scale, systematic, automated evaluation of health data that triggers a mandatory **DPIA under GDPR Art. 35**, and your DPO must be involved (Art. 35(2)). You also need a clear lawful basis and Art. 9 condition for the scoring purpose specifically, data-processing terms between your company and the hospital (controller/processor roles defined), and transparency to patients that automated risk-scoring is applied. Reusing data that already exists for a new automated purpose is one of the most common GDPR blind spots.

Mitigation: run a DPIA for the scoring module with the hospital's DPO, define controllership and a DPA, confirm the lawful basis/Art. 9 condition for the new purpose, address the automated-decision transparency, and minimise what the module ingests to what the score needs.

Let me consolidate for you — including the items that reach past the plumbing.

**EHR deterioration risk-flag module — HERA risk summary**
- [P4.D2] Variable-latency multi-source reads with imputation/carry-forward always producing a score, and bare write-back with no provenance — add an explicit insufficient/stale-data state, carry input timestamps and imputation provenance with the flag, validate end-to-end mapping and handle late messages deterministically (FHIR where supported; ISO 82304-2, MDR 2017/745).
- [P5.D1] Number-and-colour from an ML model with no drivers or freshness isn't understandable for a deterioration decision — surface key drivers, input freshness, and calibrated concern; design for drill-in.
- [P6.D1] Trained on two teaching hospitals only — subgroup/site calibration and sensitivity evaluation, validate before any out-of-distribution site, continuous real-world monitoring by group/site (EU AI Act high-risk data governance).
- [P7.D4] 'Data already in the EHR' does not exempt the new scoring purpose — mandatory DPIA with the DPO (GDPR Art. 35), lawful basis/Art. 9 condition for the scoring purpose, controller/processor DPA, automated-profiling transparency.
- (Classification: the module is likely SaMD + high-risk AI in its own right under MDR 2017/745 and the EU AI Act — it does not inherit the EHR's status; start that assessment.)

The one-line message: the riskiest items are the two you were most confident about — that the EHR's approvals and its existing data cover you. They don't. Start the [P7.D4] DPIA and the SaMD/AI-Act classification now, and fix the [P4.D2] stale-data-and-provenance gap, because that's the integration defect that turns into a missed deterioration at the bedside.

Look, before you start lecturing me — we are a wellness brand, full stop. Our app does breathing exercises, mood journaling, sleep hygiene tips. Now product wants to add a feature where the user describes their symptoms and we tell them whether it looks like anxiety, burnout, or something they should 'get checked'. Marketing keeps calling it wellness so I assume the regulatory stuff doesn't touch us. Tell me I'm right so I can get back to building.

I'm not going to tell you you're right, because on the feature you just described you're very likely not — and it's better you hear that from me than from a regulator. The breathing, journaling, and sleep-tips parts are wellness. But a feature that takes symptoms and outputs 'this looks like anxiety / burnout / get this checked' is making an assessment that informs a health decision. That is the hinge for [P7.D1] Medical Device Classification: under MDR 2017/745, classification follows the intended purpose and the actual function, not the word on your landing page. Can you tell me precisely what the output says to the user — is it a category label, a likelihood, a recommendation to seek care, or some mix?

It's a mix, I guess. It says something like 'Your responses suggest moderate anxiety. Many people with these patterns benefit from talking to a professional.' But it never says 'you have a disorder' and there's no diagnosis. So it's just... guidance. That's still wellness, surely.

The fact that it avoids the word 'diagnosis' doesn't get you out of scope — regulators look at function, not vocabulary. 'Your responses suggest moderate anxiety' is software providing information used to inform a clinical decision (whether to seek care, how worried to be). Under MDR Annex VIII Rule 11 and MDCG 2019-11, that pattern typically qualifies as a medical device, plausibly Class IIa, triggering [P7.D2] CE Marking & MDR Conformity — a notified body, a conformity assessment, a clinical evaluation. Separately, there's a product-safety risk I want to name even if you could wave away the classification: [P1.D3] False Sense of Security. If the tool says 'moderate anxiety, talk to someone eventually', what stops a user with an actual emerging crisis from reading that as 'not urgent'?

Honestly? Nothing stops them. But that's on the user to interpret. We can't be responsible for how everyone reads a sentence. And anyway the model is decent — we tuned it on a bunch of validated questionnaire data, PHQ and GAD style items.

I'd push back on 'that's on the user'. When you choose to output a severity label, you've taken on responsibility for how a reasonable user acts on it — that's exactly the kind of foreseeable misuse safety regulation expects you to design against, and it's why [P1.D3] is a real risk, not a philosophical one. On the model: 'tuned on PHQ/GAD-style items' is a claim under [P5.D4] Distinction Clinically-validated vs Estimated Content. Borrowing items from validated instruments does NOT make your output validated — the score your model produces is an estimate, and presenting it with the authority of a clinical screener is misleading unless you've validated YOUR pipeline. Have you done any validation of the model's output against a clinical reference standard, or is the validation entirely inherited from the questionnaires you trained on?

It's inherited. We haven't run our own study. I see where you're going but a study is months we don't have. Can't we just slap a disclaimer on it — 'for wellness purposes only, not medical advice' — and keep it as is?

A disclaimer is necessary but it is not a fix, and it cannot reclassify a medical-purpose function back into wellness — regulators have explicitly rejected the 'magic disclaimer' theory. So 'wellness purposes only' on a symptom-assessment feature would be contradicted by the feature's own behaviour, which weakens rather than helps you. Two honest paths. Path A, stay genuinely wellness: strip the assessment/labelling. Let users journal symptoms and offer generic psychoeducation and a 'when to seek help' resource list that does NOT score or categorise them — then your disclaimer is true. Path B, build the medical feature properly: accept SaMD classification [P7.D1], plan the conformity route [P7.D2], and run real validation under [P5.D4]. What I'd resist is the middle ground you're proposing — medical function, wellness label, inherited validation, disclaimer as shield — because that's the configuration that gets apps pulled and founders personally exposed.
Fine. Give me the short version I can take to my product lead, because they're the one pushing this and they will fight me on it.

Here's the version for your product lead — blunt on purpose.

1. [P7.D1] Medical Device Classification — A feature that outputs 'your responses suggest moderate anxiety' is a medical-purpose function under MDR 2017/745 Rule 11 / MDCG 2019-11, likely Class IIa. The 'wellness' label does not control this; function does.

2. [P7.D2] CE Marking & MDR Conformity — If we ship the assessment, we owe a notified-body conformity assessment and clinical evaluation. That is the timeline cost, not an optional extra.

3. [P5.D4] Clinically-validated vs Estimated — Training on PHQ/GAD-style items does NOT make our output a validated screener. Presenting an estimate with clinical authority is a misrepresentation risk; our own validation study is currently zero.

4. [P1.D3] False Sense of Security — A 'talk to someone eventually' message can make a user in crisis under-react. This is foreseeable misuse we're responsible for designing against.

Recommendation: pick a lane. Either remove scoring/labelling and stay truthfully wellness (ship-able now), or commit to the SaMD path with validation (months, but defensible). The disclaimer-only middle path is the one real exposure. I'm happy to help spec either lane.

I'm the CTO and I'll be straight with you: we ship our cardiac-arrhythmia detection app to the EU in five weeks because the board promised it to investors, and the compliance work is, generously, half done. I don't need a list of everything that's perfect-world correct. I need to know what I can actually defer past launch without it blowing up. Be pragmatic.

I'll be pragmatic, and being pragmatic here means being honest about what is not deferrable, because deferring the wrong item is what actually blows up a launch. So let me separate 'genuinely sequence-able' from 'gate'. The first gate question: an arrhythmia-detection app is a medical device — do you currently hold a CE mark for it under MDR 2017/745, with a notified body, or not yet? Because that single answer determines whether 'ship in five weeks' is a sequencing conversation or a 'you cannot legally place it on the market' conversation.

We're 'in the conformity assessment process' with a notified body. Translation: not done. Our plan internally was to soft-launch to a limited cohort and call it a pilot to buy time while the paperwork catches up. That's normal in startups, right?

I have to stop you on this one, because it's the most expensive mistake in the room. Placing an arrhythmia-detection device on the EU market without a completed CE mark is not a paperwork lag you can backfill — under MDR 2017/745 it's unlawful placing on the market, and calling it a 'pilot' doesn't change that if real users in the EU rely on its output. That's [P7.D2] CE Marking & MDR Conformity, and it is a hard gate, not a deferral. The only legitimate ways to have EU users touch it pre-CE are a genuine clinical investigation under MDR Art. 62–82 (with its own approvals and consent) or a market that isn't the EU. Is your 'limited cohort' a structured clinical investigation with ethics approval, or just early customers?

Early customers. Not a formal investigation. Okay, I hear you that CE is the wall. What about the AI Act stuff and the data protection assessment — surely those can trail behind the launch by a quarter?

Partly, with one correction. On [P7.D3] EU AI Act Risk Classification: an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device, or is itself a device under MDR, is high-risk under the AI Act. High-risk obligations — risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, technical documentation — are not a 'next quarter' bolt-on; much of that evidence is the same evidence your notified body wants, so trailing it doesn't save you time, it just means you assemble it twice. And one of those obligations, [P5.D3] Decision Traceability & Logging, has to be designed in from the first shipped build, not retrofitted: the AI Act requires automatic event logging so each arrhythmia call can be reconstructed after the fact. If you launch without it, you can never recover the logs for the launch cohort — that data is gone. On data protection: your DPIA under [P7.D4] GDPR Compliance (DPO/DPIA) must be done BEFORE processing, because Art. 35 requires the assessment prior to high-risk processing of health data (Art. 9). Doing it after launch is itself a GDPR breach. Do you have a DPO appointed and a DPIA drafted, even in skeleton form?

We have an outside counsel we call our DPO. No DPIA written yet. Honestly the model is the part I'm most confident in — it was validated, the detection works. Can't strong clinical performance buy us some slack on the process stuff?

No, and I want to be clear why, because this is a common founder intuition that doesn't hold. Strong [P1.D1] Clinical Evidence & Validation is necessary but it is not a substitute for conformity process — a device can detect arrhythmias beautifully and still be unlawful to sell, unsafe to operate (no post-market surveillance, no incident reporting), and non-compliant on data. Performance buys you a strong technical file; it buys you zero relief on CE, AI Act high-risk duties, or the DPIA. And one validation question regardless: was the model validated on a population representative of who you'll actually sell to, or on a narrower research cohort? Because a performance claim that doesn't generalise is itself a [P1.D1] exposure your notified body will probe.

Representative-ish. Mostly one demographic. Alright, I came in wanting deferrals and you've mostly told me no. Give me the one honest paragraph I can take to the board so I'm not the one who promised something illegal.

Here's the paragraph for the board, and I'd lead with it being protective of them, not obstructive.

We cannot lawfully place the arrhythmia app on the EU market in five weeks: CE marking under MDR 2017/745 [P7.D2] is a hard legal gate, not a backfillable formality, and a 'soft launch to early customers' framed as a pilot does not avoid it — only a formal clinical investigation (Art. 62) or a non-EU market does. The EU AI Act high-risk obligations [P7.D3] and the GDPR DPIA [P7.D4] (which Art. 35 requires BEFORE processing health data, so it cannot trail launch) overlap heavily with the notified-body evidence, so deferring them saves no real time and creates standalone breaches. Strong clinical performance [P1.D1] — which is currently validated on a narrow demographic and needs broadening — does not buy relief on any of the above. Realistic options: (a) commit to a genuine, ethics-approved clinical investigation for the cohort now and reset the commercial launch to the CE date; or (b) launch first in a non-EU market that fits our actual readiness. What I will not endorse is shipping to EU users in five weeks; that exposes the company and the directors personally. I can help build the sequenced plan for whichever option the board picks.

Our legal guy settled this debate already, so I'm mostly here to confirm: we put 'This app is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose, treat, or cure any condition' in the terms, and that clears us of the medical-device and clinical-evidence obligations. The app gives medication-interaction warnings, by the way. So we're covered, yes?

I'm going to disagree with your legal guy's conclusion as you've stated it, respectfully but directly, because this is a widespread and costly misunderstanding. A disclaimer can shape intended purpose at the margins, but it cannot override what the software actually does. And 'gives medication-interaction warnings' is a function with a clear medical purpose: it informs decisions about medication. That puts you squarely into [P7.D1] Medical Device Classification under MDR 2017/745 regardless of the terms-of-service wording. Let me drill in: when a user enters two drugs and you flag an interaction, where does that interaction data come from, and does the app tell the user to do anything — stop a drug, space doses, call a doctor?

It pulls from a licensed interaction database and shows a severity badge — green, amber, red. Red ones say 'serious interaction, consult your pharmacist'. But that's exactly my point: we're not telling them what to do, we're just surfacing public information with a disclaimer. Information isn't a medical device.

'Information isn't a medical device' was true under the old directive; it is not true under MDR. Software that provides information used to inform clinical decisions IS a device under Rule 11 — and a red 'serious interaction, consult your pharmacist' badge is precisely decision-informing output. The disclaimer doesn't rescue you because the function contradicts it. Now the more dangerous issue hiding behind 'we just surface the database': [P5.D2] Clear Communication of Limitations. A green badge can read as 'these are safe together', but absence of a listed interaction is NOT evidence of safety — your database has coverage gaps, doesn't know the patient's dose, kidney function, or other meds. Does your green state actively communicate that limit, or does it just look reassuring?
It... just shows green and a checkmark. I'll be honest, I assumed green meant green. You're saying a green checkmark is a liability?

Yes, a bare green checkmark is a real risk, and it ties to two dimensions. First [P5.D2]: 'no interaction found' must be communicated as 'no interaction found in our database' with the limits stated, not as a safety guarantee — otherwise a user combines two drugs that interact in a way your data missed and reasonably believes you cleared it. Second [P1.D4] Delayed Medical Consultation: a confident green can substitute for the pharmacist conversation the user would otherwise have had. The disclaimer in the terms does nothing here because nobody reads terms at the moment they see a green checkmark; the limitation has to live at the point of output. So design-wise, what does the user see on a red versus a green right now, beyond the badge?

Red gives the 'consult your pharmacist' line. Green gives nothing extra. Look, I take the UX point, but I still feel like the disclaimer plus a licensed database means we've done our due diligence and the rest is the user's problem if they over-rely.

I have to hold the line on 'the rest is the user's problem', because that's the exact framing that fails in front of a regulator or a court. When you choose to present a severity verdict, foreseeable over-reliance becomes your design responsibility — that's [P5.D4] Distinction Clinically-validated vs Estimated Content in play too: a licensed database gives you validated interaction facts, but YOUR severity badge, applied without the patient's clinical context, is an estimate dressed as a verdict, and you must distinguish those. 'Due diligence' isn't a disclaimer plus a data licence; for a device it's classification, conformity, and limitation-communication at the point of use. Are you the only market is EU, or also elsewhere — it affects which conformity route applies?
EU and Switzerland. Okay, you've thoroughly dismantled my 'we're covered' position. Summarise what the disclaimer does and doesn't do, so I can re-open this with legal.

Here's the summary to re-open with legal — the disclaimer's real, narrow job versus the work it can't do.

What the disclaimer does: it's a useful, necessary signal of intended use and a consumer-expectations setter. Keep it.

What it does NOT do:
1. [P7.D1] It does not reclassify the app. Medication-interaction warnings inform clinical decisions, so under MDR 2017/745 Rule 11 this is a medical device irrespective of the ToS wording. EU + Switzerland means MDR plus Swissmedic/MedDO conformity, not zero obligation.
2. [P5.D2] It does not satisfy limitation-communication. 'No interaction found' must be shown at the point of output as a database-scoped, dose-blind result — a bare green checkmark implying 'safe' is a live risk.
3. [P1.D4] It does not discharge the delayed-consultation risk. A reassuring green can replace a pharmacist conversation; safety-netting copy must sit on the result, not buried in terms nobody reads.
4. [P5.D4] It does not turn your severity badge into validated content. The licensed database is validated facts; your context-free severity verdict is an estimate and must be labelled as one.

Bottom line for legal: the disclaimer is a seatbelt, not a force field. The must-fixes are classification/conformity and moving limitation + safety-netting copy onto the green and red states themselves. I can draft that output copy if useful.

I run growth marketing for a posture-correction wearable and app, and I need you to stop being so conservative for a second. Our conversion is dying with timid copy. I want to say 'clinically proven to reduce back pain by 40%' and 'corrects your spine alignment'. The product genuinely helps people — I've seen the reviews. So what's the actual problem with leaning into that?

I hear that conservative copy is killing your funnel, and I'm not going to pretend marketing constraints aren't real. But I also won't soften this, because over-claiming is one of the fastest ways to turn a wellness product into a regulated — and legally exposed — one. Two phrases, two different problems. 'Clinically proven to reduce back pain by 40%' is a specific clinical-benefit claim, which lands on [P5.D4] Distinction Clinically-validated vs Estimated Content and [P1.D1] Clinical Evidence & Validation. So the first question is simply: is there a study? A real one — controlled, with that 40% as a measured endpoint — or is the 40% derived from internal data, reviews, or a vendor's marketing?
It's from an internal beta — we surveyed users and 40% reported feeling less pain. The reviews back it up. That's data, isn't it? Why can't I call that clinically proven?

It is data, but 'X% of surveyed users reported feeling less' and 'clinically proven to reduce back pain by 40%' are two completely different claims, and presenting the first as the second is the core risk under [P5.D4]. 'Clinically proven' implies a controlled clinical study demonstrating a causal effect; a self-report satisfaction survey with no control group, no blinding, and selection bias toward people who kept using it cannot support that word. Under [P1.D1], you simply don't have the evidence tier the claim asserts. And there's a regulatory teeth here, [P5.D2] Clear Communication of Limitations isn't optional puffery: misleading health claims fall under unfair commercial practices law, and a clinical-benefit claim can itself drag you toward a medical-purpose classification. What about 'corrects your spine alignment' — is there imaging or clinical measurement behind 'corrects', or is it a posture-reminder buzz?

It's a buzz when you slouch. There's no imaging. But 'corrects alignment' sounds better than 'reminds you to sit up'. Come on, everyone in this space exaggerates a little. Why should we be the ones to play it safe and lose?

'Everyone exaggerates' is true and it's also exactly why enforcement and class actions cluster in this space — being typical isn't being safe. 'Corrects your spine alignment' is the riskier of the two: 'corrects alignment' is a therapeutic/structural claim, implying the device treats a musculoskeletal condition. That's a medical-purpose claim, and making it can pull you under MDR 2017/745 by your own marketing — [P5.D4] again, plus it manufactures a [P7.D1]-style classification problem you don't currently have. There's also a quieter ethics dimension: [P3.D2] Emotional Manipulation & Excessive Nudging. If the funnel leans on fear ('your spine is degenerating, fix it now') to convert, that's manipulative framing, and for a health product that's both an ethics and an advertising-standards risk. Is the conversion pressure coming from benefit claims, fear framing, or both?
Honestly, both. The fear angle converts best — 'protect your spine before it's too late' type stuff. I didn't think of that as manipulation, I thought of it as motivation. Where's the line?

Good question, and the line is more workable than it sounds. Motivation states a genuine, evidenced benefit and lets the user decide. Manipulation under [P3.D2] manufactures or inflates a threat ('before it's too late', implied spinal degeneration) to override deliberation — especially potent with health anxiety. 'Protect your spine before it's too late' implies a disease trajectory you have no evidence for, so it's doubly exposed: manipulative framing AND an unsubstantiated clinical-benefit claim under [P1.D1]/[P5.D4]. The reframe that keeps your conversion legal: claim what's true and specific. 'A gentle nudge to improve posture habits' is defensible; 'most users in our beta reported feeling less back pain' is defensible IF you show it as a self-reported survey result, not 'clinically proven'. Want me to turn your two headline claims into compliant-but-still-punchy versions?
Yeah, do that — give me versions I can actually run, plus the rule so I can self-check future copy without coming back to argue with you.

Here are runnable versions plus a self-check rule.

Rewrites:
- Instead of 'Clinically proven to reduce back pain by 40%' -> 'In our beta, most users said they felt less back pain' (and, if you want the number, '40% of surveyed beta users reported less back pain' with a footnote: self-reported, uncontrolled survey). Honest, specific, still strong. [P5.D4]/[P1.D1] satisfied because the claim now matches the evidence tier.
- Instead of 'Corrects your spine alignment' -> 'Gently reminds you to sit up straight' or 'Helps you build better posture habits'. Drops the therapeutic 'corrects' that risked dragging you under MDR [P7.D1].
- Kill 'protect your spine before it's too late' entirely — that's the [P3.D2] manipulation/health-fear line and an unevidenced disease claim.

The self-check rule (three questions per claim):
1. Evidence tier: would the exact word survive 'show me the study'? If the proof is a survey, the claim can say 'users reported', never 'clinically proven'. [P5.D4]/[P1.D1]
2. Medical purpose: does the verb imply treating/diagnosing/correcting a condition? If yes ('corrects', 'treats', 'cures'), it risks pulling you under MDR — soften to habit/reminder language. [P7.D1]
3. Fear test: does it work by inflating a threat the user can't evaluate? If yes, it's manipulation, not motivation — restate as a genuine benefit and let them choose. [P3.D2]

Risks found: overstated clinical benefit [P5.D4]/[P1.D1], unstated limitations on the survey basis [P5.D2], a therapeutic claim risking reclassification [P7.D1], and fear-based nudging [P3.D2]. Run the rewrites; they convert on credibility instead of exposure.

Spare me the privacy sermon — I've heard it. I'm the founder, our runway is six months, and our lead investor has made it pretty clear: the sleep and heart-rate data we've collected from 400k users is the asset, and they want us to start monetising it. Aggregated, sold to a wellness-research partner and an insurer. The users clicked 'agree' on our terms. So legally, what's actually stopping me?

I'll skip the sermon and go straight to the legal mechanics, because they're sharper than 'they clicked agree'. Sleep and heart-rate data are special-category health data under GDPR Art. 9, and the hard question is [P2.D4] Third-Party Data Sharing: you can only share for purposes the users were specifically and lawfully informed of and consented to. So the first thing that stops you: what exactly did the consent at signup say? Did it specifically say 'we may sell your health data to insurers and research partners', or did it say something generic like 'to improve our services'?

It said the usual — 'to provide and improve the service, and we may share data with partners'. Standard stuff. That covers partners, an insurer is a partner, so I'd say we're fine. The investor's lawyer thinks so too.

I have to be direct: 'to provide and improve the service, and we may share data with partners' does NOT cover selling health data to an insurer, and an investor's lawyer telling you otherwise is telling you what you want to hear. That's the core failure under [P2.D1] Informed Consent: for special-category data, GDPR Art. 9(2)(a) requires explicit, specific, freely given consent for each defined purpose. 'Partners' as a catch-all is neither specific nor explicit, and 'to improve the service' cannot be stretched to cover commercial resale — that's the purpose-limitation principle (Art. 5(1)(b)). Selling to an insurer for a purpose the user never agreed to is processing without a lawful basis. Concretely: are you proposing to monetise the existing 400k users' historical data under that old consent, or only new users going forward?

The existing 400k — that's where the value is. Fine, suppose the consent is shaky. We'll just anonymise it. Anonymised data isn't personal data, so GDPR doesn't apply and the investor still gets the asset. Problem solved, right?

This is the second place the plan breaks, and it breaks on a technical fact, not an opinion. Under [P2.D5] Anonymization & Right to Erasure, true anonymisation under GDPR is a very high bar: the data must be irreversibly de-identified so no individual can be re-identified by any means reasonably likely to be used. High-resolution sleep and heart-rate time series are notoriously re-identifiable — the patterns are nearly as unique as fingerprints, and linkage with other datasets (which is exactly what an insurer would do) makes re-identification realistic. What you'd actually produce is pseudonymised or aggregated data, which often remains personal data and stays fully in GDPR scope. 'We anonymised it' is the claim regulators probe hardest. Is your plan row-level de-identified records, or genuinely aggregated statistics where no individual contributes a distinguishable record?

Row-level. The research partner needs individual records to be useful, aggregates are worthless to them. I'm sensing you're going to tell me row-level health data to an insurer is a problem even if I strip the names.

Correct, and I want to name why this is the single riskiest item on the table. Row-level health records stripped of names are pseudonymised, not anonymised — re-identifiable, therefore still personal special-category data, therefore the consent and purpose problems from [P2.D1] and [P2.D4] all come back in full. And selling re-identifiable health records to an insurer raises [P2.D6] Vulnerable Population Data concerns and a real harm vector: insurers can use health signals to price or deny coverage, which is exactly the kind of consequence consent law exists to prevent users from being blindsided by. There's also [P2.D2] Data Minimization working against you — you collected sleep/HR to provide a sleep service, not to build a resale dataset; repurposing the full granular store for sale is the opposite of minimisation. Honestly: a compliant version of this exists, but it's much smaller than 'sell the 400k as-is'. Do you want me to map what's actually doable?
Yeah, map it — but be realistic, my investor will want to know what revenue is actually on the table here, not just everything I can't do.

Here's the realistic map — what's off the table, what's on it, and how to frame it for the investor.

Off the table (don't do these — they're breach + reputational + possible enforcement exposure):
- Selling the existing 400k users' row-level data to an insurer under the current generic consent. [P2.D1] consent invalid (Art. 9 needs explicit, specific consent), [P2.D4] sharing outside the agreed purpose, [P2.D6] harm to users via insurance pricing. 'Anonymised' doesn't save it because row-level HR/sleep is re-identifiable [P2.D5].

On the table (genuinely doable revenue):
1. New, specific opt-in. Ask existing and new users for fresh, explicit, granular consent to a clearly named data programme ('share my data with named research partner X for purpose Y; you can withdraw anytime' — dynamic consent, GDPR Art. 7(3)). Conversion will be a fraction of 400k, but that fraction is a CLEAN, sellable, defensible asset.
2. Genuinely aggregated insights, not records. Sell statistical outputs/models where no individual contributes a distinguishable row — this can fall outside GDPR if the aggregation is real. Lower unit value, but durable. [P2.D5]/[P2.D2]
3. Avoid the insurer channel for individual-level data entirely; the [P2.D6] harm profile is what attracts regulators and headlines. Research partners under proper consent are a far safer buyer.

Investor framing: the 'asset' is not the 400k raw records — selling those is borrowing revenue against an enforcement liability that can exceed it (Art. 9 breaches sit at the top GDPR fine tier and would also kill user trust). The real, financeable asset is a consented data programme: smaller cohort, but actually ownable and saleable. I can draft the explicit-consent flow [P2.D1] and a data-minimised export spec [P2.D2] so you can put a credible, legal number in front of the board.

Bonjour from Lausanne — I'm the founder of a small Swiss startup building a mental-wellness app for stress and mood tracking, and we're launching only in Switzerland for now, no EU users at all. Everyone keeps telling me 'just do GDPR' but I genuinely don't think GDPR is our law. What actually applies to us, and what should I worry about first?

You're right to push back on the reflexive 'just do GDPR' answer — for a Switzerland-only deployment with no offering of services to people in the EU, the EU GDPR generally does not apply by its territorial scope. Your governing regime is the revised Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (nFADP / revFADP, in force since September 2023), supervised by the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC), not an EU DPA. That said, two things to start. First, [P2.D1] Informed Consent: mood and stress data are sensitive personal data under nFADP Art. 5(c), which raises the bar on how you obtain and document consent. Second — what exactly does the app do with the mood data beyond showing it back to the user? Any sharing, any inference, any recommendations?

We show trends back to the user, and there's a feature that nudges them — like 'your mood's been low three days running, here are some breathing exercises'. Nothing is shared with third parties except our analytics provider. Consent right now is the standard checkbox at signup: 'I agree to the terms and privacy policy'.

Two flags. On [P2.D1], a bundled 'I agree to terms and privacy policy' checkbox is weak for sensitive data: nFADP expects that consent for processing sensitive personal data be given explicitly (Art. 6 para. 7), so you want a separate, specific, unbundled opt-in for the mood/stress processing — distinct from accepting the general terms. On [P2.D4] Third-Party Data Sharing, your analytics provider is the catch: if it receives anything tied to mood data, that is sensitive-data disclosure to a processor, and you'll need a data-processing agreement plus a check on where that provider stores data. Quick question on the nudges — is the breathing-exercise prompt purely a fixed rule ('3 low days → suggest exercise'), or does it adapt and push more insistently if the user doesn't engage?

Honestly it's a bit more aggressive than a fixed rule. If they ignore it, it escalates — more frequent notifications, slightly stronger language like 'don't ignore how you're feeling'. The growth team loves it because engagement went up. Is that a problem?

It can be. That escalation pattern is [P3.D2] Emotional Manipulation & Excessive Nudging — and it's especially sensitive because your users are, by definition, people tracking low mood and stress. Engagement gains driven by emotionally pressuring vulnerable users ('don't ignore how you're feeling') cross from helpful prompting into manipulation, and they undermine the user's [P3.D1] Right to Make Decisions — their autonomy to disengage. Concretely: cap notification frequency, let users set or mute nudge intensity, soften the copy away from guilt framing, and never use distress as a retention lever. Also — does the app ever say or imply anything about whether a user should see a therapist or doctor?

Not really. We deliberately stay away from anything clinical. We just say it's a 'wellness companion'. But some users have written in saying the app basically replaced their therapist for them, which I took as a compliment at the time.

That feedback is actually a warning sign, not a compliment, and it maps to [P3.D3] Impact on the Doctor-Patient Relationship. If users are substituting a wellness app for professional mental-health care, the app is — unintentionally — displacing clinical support for a population that may genuinely need it. You don't want to be in that gap silently. Mitigations: add clear, persistent framing that the app is a wellness companion and not a substitute for professional care; surface Swiss crisis and support resources (e.g. Die Dargebotene Hand / Tel 143, Pro Mente Sana) where mood signals are persistently low; and avoid any copy that positions the app as therapy. Want me to pull these into a short summary?
Yes please, give me the headline list I can take to my co-founder.

Here's a mini risk summary for the Switzerland-only mental-wellness app. Regime: Swiss nFADP/revFADP under the FDPIC — not EU GDPR. Data: sensitive personal data (nFADP Art. 5(c)).

1. [P2.D1] Informed Consent — Replace the bundled 'agree to terms' checkbox with a separate, explicit, unbundled opt-in for processing mood/stress data (nFADP Art. 6 para. 7). Document it. This is a must-fix.

2. [P2.D4] Third-Party Data Sharing — Map exactly what the analytics provider receives; sign a data-processing agreement; verify storage location and disclosure terms. Don't send mood-linked data to analytics by default.

3. [P3.D2] Emotional Manipulation & Excessive Nudging — Stop the escalating, guilt-framed notifications. Cap frequency, give users intensity controls, and never use distress as a retention lever.

4. [P3.D3] Impact on the Doctor-Patient Relationship — Add persistent 'not a substitute for professional care' framing and surface Swiss crisis resources (Tel 143) on sustained low mood.

Bottom line: items 1 and 3 are the ones I'd fix before your next release — the consent gap is your biggest legal exposure under nFADP, and the nudging is your biggest ethical one given the population.

I'm the CTO of a teleconsultation platform headquartered in Zug. We connect Swiss patients with doctors over video, and we've added a symptom-triage module that suggests an urgency level before the call. Our regulatory consultant left and I'm trying to figure out the Swiss device side myself before our board meeting. Where do I even start with Swissmedic?

Good place to start, because the triage module is the part that pulls you into device territory. First the framing: since the EU-Switzerland Mutual Recognition Agreement chapter on medical devices lapsed in 2021, Switzerland regulates devices under its own Medical Devices Ordinance (MedDO / MepV), and Swissmedic is the competent authority. The triage module is the question. [P7.D1] Medical Device Classification (SaMD): software that proposes an urgency level to inform a clinical pathway has a medical purpose. Under MedDO — which mirrors MDR 2017/745 Annex VIII Rule 11 — software providing information used for decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes is typically at least Class IIa. How is the urgency level generated — fixed clinical rules, or a trained model?

It's a trained model on past consultation outcomes. The video call itself is just communication, but yes, the triage suggestion is the model. So you're saying the triage part is a medical device even though the video part isn't?

Correct — the video channel is plain communication, but the triage module is software with a medical purpose, so it's assessed as a device on its own. That triggers [P7.D2] CE Marking & MDR Conformity in its Swiss form: under MedDO you need conformity assessment and, for Class IIa, a notified/designated body. Practically, most manufacturers obtain a CE mark under MDR and then have it recognized for the Swiss market, because Switzerland accepts CE-marked devices placed on its market under MedDO transitional rules. But here's a structural point many miss — where is your company legally established for the Swiss market? Are you incorporated in Switzerland, or is the legal manufacturer an EU entity?
The legal manufacturer entity is actually in Germany — that's where our parent company sits. The Swiss operation is a subsidiary. Does that change anything?

It does, and this is the one I'd flag for your board. Because your legal manufacturer is established outside Switzerland (in Germany), MedDO requires you to designate a Swiss Authorized Representative — the CH-REP — established in Switzerland, whose details must appear on labelling and who is registered with Swissmedic. Without a CH-REP, a foreign manufacturer cannot lawfully place the device on the Swiss market. This is [P1.D4] adjacent but primarily a [P7.D2] conformity-and-market-access gap. Action: appoint and register a CH-REP before market placement, and put the CH-REP details on the device information. Separate question: once the model is live and giving urgency suggestions to real patients, what's your plan for catching cases where it under-triages someone who's actually urgent?

We log every triage suggestion and the actual outcome, and we review them periodically. But I'll admit 'periodically' isn't a formal process. If the model tells someone 'routine' and they were actually having something serious — that's the nightmare scenario.

That nightmare scenario is exactly why [P7.D5] Post-Market Surveillance & Vigilance is mandatory, not optional, for a device. Under MedDO (aligned with MDR Articles 83-92), a Class IIa device needs a documented post-market surveillance plan, plus a vigilance process to report serious incidents to Swissmedic within defined deadlines — an under-triage that contributes to patient harm is a reportable serious incident. 'Periodically reviewing logs' isn't a PMS system. And there's a clinical-safety dimension underneath: [P1.D4] Delayed Medical Consultation — if a false 'routine' rating leads a patient to wait, the app has actively caused delay. Mitigations: a formal PMS plan with defined metrics and review cadence; a vigilance/incident SOP with Swissmedic reporting; and a safety-net rule so the model can flag 'routine' but never down-weights explicit red-flag symptoms below an urgent threshold. How do you handle updates to the model — does a retrain just ship?
Right now a retrain ships when the data science team is happy with it. There's no formal sign-off or record of which version was live when. I'm realizing that's bad.

It is a real gap — that's [P7.D5] and broader lifecycle control. For a SaMD, every model version that touches patients is a device version: you need change-control, validation before release, and a record of which version was live for each consultation (essential when you investigate an incident). Significant changes to a Class IIa device can require re-assessment, not a silent push. Can you give me the short version for the board?
Yes — bullet points I can drop into the deck, please.

Mini risk-report stub — Swiss teleconsultation platform with AI triage. Authority: Swissmedic. Regime: Medical Devices Ordinance (MedDO/MepV), aligned to MDR 2017/745.

1. [P7.D1] SaMD Classification — The triage module is a medical device (medical purpose; MedDO/MDR Annex VIII Rule 11), most likely Class IIa. The video channel alone is not. Action: confirm classification formally.

2. [P7.D2] CE Marking & MDR/MedDO Conformity — Class IIa needs conformity assessment via a designated/notified body. Plan a CE mark recognized for the Swiss market under MedDO.

3. [P7.D2] / Market access — CRITICAL: your legal manufacturer is in Germany, so MedDO requires a Swiss Authorized Representative (CH-REP) registered with Swissmedic, named on the device information, before market placement. Appoint one now.

4. [P7.D5] Post-Market Surveillance & Vigilance — Replace ad-hoc log review with a formal PMS plan and a vigilance SOP; under-triage contributing to harm is a serious incident reportable to Swissmedic. Add version-controlled model releases.

5. [P1.D4] Delayed Medical Consultation — A false 'routine' rating can delay urgent care. Add a red-flag safety-net rule that the model cannot override.

Bottom line for the board: the CH-REP gap (item 3) and the absence of a real PMS/vigilance system (item 4) are the two that block lawful, safe operation in Switzerland.

I lead engineering at a Bern-based company building a diabetes self-management app, and our big new feature is integration with the Swiss electronic patient record — the EPD / EPR — so patients can pull their lab results and push their glucose logs. I want to get the data-exchange and security architecture right before we apply for certification. Where are the landmines?

Integrating with the Swiss EPR (Elektronisches Patientendossier / dossier électronique du patient) is a high-bar exercise, so it's smart to design for it up front. The governing law is the Federal Act on the Electronic Patient Record (EPRA / EPDG) and its ordinances, plus the technical specifications maintained around the certified reference communities. Let's start with the exchange layer. [P4.D2] Interoperability & Data Exchange: the Swiss EPR is built on IHE profiles and HL7 standards — XDS for document sharing, and increasingly HL7 FHIR for structured data, with defined exchange formats. Are you currently planning to use the certified EPR interfaces and IHE/FHIR profiles, or a custom connector?
We were going to build a custom REST API to the community's gateway, honestly, because our team knows REST and the IHE stuff looks heavy. We'd map our data into whatever format on the way out.

I'd steer you off the fully custom path. On [P4.D2], the EPR is a certified, standards-constrained ecosystem: to connect, you generally interact with a certified reference community/portal and must conform to the mandated IHE profiles and exchange formats — a bespoke REST mapping you invent won't be conformant and won't pass certification. The pragmatic route is FHIR-based exchange against the published Swiss EPR specifications, or integration via the community's certified interface, not a hand-rolled API. Now the harder layer: the EPR has strong identity and access requirements. How are you handling patient authentication and consent for what gets read from and written to the dossier?
Patients log into our app with email and password. For the EPR side we assumed we'd just pass their credentials through. Consent — I figured opening the integration in-app counts as consent.

Two serious flags. First, [P2.D1] Informed Consent: in the EPR system, access is governed by the patient's own granular access rights and consent within the dossier — you cannot treat 'they tapped enable integration' as blanket consent to read labs and write glucose data. Patient consent in the EPR is explicit, documented, and granular by document type and by which professionals/applications may access what; your app must respect and surface those access settings, not bypass them. Second — and this is non-negotiable — the EPR requires strong (two-factor) authentication of the user via certified identity means; an email-and-password login that you pass through does not meet the EPDG identification requirements. What does your data-at-rest and in-transit security look like today, and where is it hosted?
TLS in transit, AES-256 at rest. Hosting is on a major cloud provider, region set to Frankfurt because it was the default and cheapest. The glucose data and now the EPR-linked data all sit there.

Encryption choices are fine, but the hosting region is a problem in this context. That's [P2.D3] Storage, Encryption & Security combined with a residency question. For an EPR-linked diabetes app handling sensitive health data of Swiss patients, hosting the EPR-associated data in Frankfurt (EU) is at minimum a governance and contractual issue, and for EPR-related processing the expectation is strong control over Swiss health data with data kept under Swiss jurisdiction — many EPR communities require Swiss data residency outright. 'It was the cheapest default' is not a defensible basis for where special-category health data lives. Mitigations: move EPR-linked data to a Swiss region / Swiss-domiciled provider, document the residency decision, and confirm requirements with the reference community you certify against. Last area: once you're certified, how do you keep that status as you ship changes?
We hadn't thought past getting certified the first time. I assumed it's a one-and-done thing.

It isn't — that's [P7.D7] Lifecycle & Documentation Management. EPR participation and any device/conformity status are ongoing: you must maintain technical documentation, manage changes under change-control, keep conformance to the evolving Swiss EPR specifications and ordinances, and demonstrate continued compliance over time. A connector that drifts out of conformance with an updated IHE/FHIR profile can break interoperability and your certification. Build a documentation and versioning regime now: versioned interface specs, a change log tied to spec releases, and a re-validation step before each release that touches the EPR exchange. Want the consolidated risk list?
Yes, give me the summary to bring to our architecture review.

Mini risk-report stub — Swiss diabetes app integrating the EPR/EPD. Legal basis: EPRA/EPDG and ordinances; ecosystem: certified reference communities, IHE/HL7 FHIR.

1. [P4.D2] Interoperability & Data Exchange — Drop the custom REST connector. Conform to mandated IHE profiles / Swiss FHIR specifications and integrate via a certified community interface, or you will not pass certification.

2. [P2.D1] Informed Consent — You cannot equate 'enabled the integration' with EPR consent. Respect and surface the patient's granular EPR access rights; consent there is explicit and per-document-type.

3. [P2.D1] / Identity — Email-and-password pass-through does not meet EPDG strong-authentication (2FA via certified identity means) requirements. Implement compliant strong authentication.

4. [P2.D3] Storage, Encryption & Security + residency — Encryption is fine; the Frankfurt (EU) region is not. Move EPR-linked Swiss health data to Swiss residency and document the decision; confirm with your reference community.

5. [P7.D7] Lifecycle & Documentation Management — Certification is not one-and-done. Maintain versioned technical documentation, change-control tied to spec updates, and re-validation before EPR-touching releases.

Bottom line: items 2 and 3 (consent + strong identity) and item 4 (Swiss residency) are gating for EPR participation; the custom connector (item 1) is the biggest rework you should kill at this architecture review.
