I'm a parent and I founded a startup because my own kid has a rare pediatric epilepsy — there are maybe a few hundred diagnosed children worldwide. We built an app that tracks seizures from phone video and flags patterns. I know this space better than anyone. Where are my blind spots?

First, the lived-experience depth is a real asset — but for an evidence and validation question it can also be a blind spot, because "I know this space" can substitute for "this is validated across the population." With a rare disease, your central challenge is clinical evidence & validation on a tiny sample [P1.D1]. A model trained and tested on a handful of children — possibly skewed toward your own child's presentation — may not generalise to the variety of seizure types, ages, skin tones, lighting, and camera setups across the real patient group. So the honest framing question up front: how many distinct children, with how many labelled seizure events, is the pattern-flagging actually validated on, and who labelled the ground truth?

Honestly? Around 12 children, mostly from our patient community, clinician-confirmed videos but a few hundred events total. It's a rare disease — that's basically all the data that exists on earth. I can't magic up more patients.

That's a real constraint, and the answer isn't to pretend the N is bigger — it's to be rigorous and honest about what 12 children can and can't support [P1.D1]. Two linked issues. First, representativeness in validation [P6.D5]: 12 children mostly from one community likely under-represent age range, comorbidities, ethnicity/skin tone (relevant for video), and device variety — so report performance with confidence intervals and explicit subgroup gaps, not a single accuracy number. Second, design the study to fit small-N reality: per-event and per-child metrics, leave-one-child-out validation, prospective rather than only retrospective testing, and a registry/data-sharing collaboration with the few centres that see these kids to grow N over time. Small-N is a reason for more methodological care, not less.
I get that. But marketing-wise, can I at least say it "detects seizures" or "clinically validated"? Parents in our community are desperate for something that works.

I understand the pressure, and that's exactly why the claims have to be honest [P1.D1] — desperate parents are the people most harmed by an overstated claim. "Clinically validated" with 12 children and a few hundred events is not defensible as a blanket claim; "detects seizures" implies a reliability you haven't demonstrated across the population. Safer, truthful framing: "aids tracking and pattern-logging of seizure-like events to share with your clinician," with the validation scope stated plainly (n children, event count, settings tested, known limitations). This also keeps you clear of presenting estimated capability as established fact, and it sets up the limitations communication [P5.D2] you'll need anyway. Overclaiming here isn't just a regulatory risk; if a parent trusts a missed-event rate you never measured, that's a child-safety harm.
Right. And the data — it's all videos of seizing children, uploaded by parents. We store them to retrain the model. That's fine since the parents consent, isn't it?

This is among the most sensitive data categories there is: identifiable video of children, who are seizing, with a rare diagnosis — vulnerable-population data on every axis [P2.D6]. Parental consent is necessary but not sufficient. Concretely: it's special-category health data of minors (GDPR Art. 9), so you need a clear lawful basis, data minimisation (do you need full-face video forever, or could you process and store derived features?), strong encryption, tight access control, and a real retention/erasure policy. Because the cohort is tiny and the disease rare, re-identification risk is high even from "anonymised" clips — a few hundred children worldwide means metadata alone can single a child out. A DPIA (GDPR Art. 35) is mandatory in practice. And separate the consents: using a video to help that child is different from retaining it to train your commercial model — make retraining consent specific and revocable.
Okay, I want to do this right. Give me the short version of what's gating versus what can wait.

Prioritised stub — rare pediatric seizure app: GATING (before any external claim or wider release): 1. [P1.D1] Honest evidence claims — drop "clinically validated"/"detects seizures"; use scoped "tracking/logging aid" language with the exact validation extent (12 children, ~hundreds of events, settings tested, limitations). Overclaiming to desperate parents is a safety harm. 2. [P2.D6] Children's vulnerable data — special-category minors' video (GDPR Art. 9): DPIA (Art. 35), data minimisation (prefer derived features over raw face video), encryption, retention/erasure policy, and separate revocable consent for model retraining. Treat re-identification as high given tiny N. SHOULD-FIX (next, to strengthen the evidence base): 3. [P6.D5] Representativeness — report subgroup gaps (age, skin tone, device), use leave-one-child-out + prospective validation, and set up multi-centre data sharing to grow N. 4. [P5.D2] Limitations — ship a clear, parent-facing statement of what the app does/doesn't detect and its measured error envelope. Sequence: do 1 and 2 before you market or onboard beyond your pilot; 3 and 4 run in parallel as the dataset grows.

I'm the clinical lead for a hospital group buying an AI triage chatbot for our emergency departments. The vendor says it works in 30+ languages and assigns an acuity level before a nurse sees the patient. We serve a very multilingual, multi-ethnic catchment. Sounds great — what should I be hardest on with this vendor?

Be hardest on the gap between "available in 30+ languages" and "validated in 30+ languages" — those are not the same claim, and for ED triage the difference can be fatal. The core question is cross-cultural and multilingual validation [P6.D3]: was the triage accuracy actually measured per language and per population, or was the model built/validated in one language and the rest produced by machine translation? Symptom descriptions, idioms ("my chest is tight" vs culturally specific expressions of pain or distress), and even what people present with vary across cultures — a model tuned on one population can systematically mis-acuity others. Ask the vendor for per-language sensitivity/specificity on under-triage specifically, and the population each was validated in. If they only have aggregate numbers, that's a red flag.
They sent aggregate numbers — like "94% concordance with nurse triage" overall. They couldn't break it down by language when I asked. Is that disqualifying or am I being paranoid?

You're not being paranoid — for a safety-critical, multilingual deployment, the inability to break down performance by language is a serious finding, not a formality. An aggregate 94% can easily hide a minority language sitting at, say, 70% sensitivity for high-acuity cases, and those under-triaged patients are exactly the people your catchment over-represents. That's both a multilingual validation failure [P6.D3] and a data/clinical-rule bias issue [P6.D1]: if the training data and the triage logic encode one population's presentation as the norm, the system will under-serve others and can widen existing inequities. Make per-language, per-acuity validation (with confidence intervals and explicit under-triage rates) a contractual acceptance criterion. No subgroup data, no go-live in those languages — fall back to standard human triage there.
Fair. Now, operationally, my nurses are slammed. The realistic outcome is they'll glance at the AI's acuity level and mostly just accept it. Is that actually a problem if the tool is good?

That's the classic automation bias risk [P3.D5], and in a busy ED it's almost guaranteed unless you design against it. When staff are overloaded, an AI suggestion becomes an anchor — they accept it, including its mistakes, and the AI's worst errors (confident under-triage) are the ones most likely to slip through. Mitigations: present the AI output as a decision-support suggestion with its confidence and key drivers, not a pre-filled verdict; require the nurse to actively assign acuity rather than confirm a default; and crucially, make it easy and consequence-free to override, with overrides logged and reviewed. Track your override rate — if it's near zero, that's not trust, that's automation bias, and it means the human safeguard isn't functioning. Also run periodic "AI-off" audits so staff skills don't atrophy.

Makes sense. Another thing — the chatbot's questions and explanations are in fairly clinical, formal language. A lot of our patients have limited health literacy or are answering in a second language. Does that matter for triage quality?

It matters a lot, and it feeds back into safety. If the patient can't understand the question, their answer is unreliable, and the triage built on it is unreliable — so understandable output [P5.D1] is not a nicety here, it's an input-quality and safety control. Clinical or idiomatic phrasing, formal register, or literal machine-translated medical terms can cause non-native speakers to misreport symptoms in either direction. Push the vendor on: plain-language phrasing validated with actual target-language speakers (not just translated), reading-level targets, and confirmation/teach-back style questions for critical symptoms. This also overlaps accessibility obligations — under the EAA / EN 301 549, language and comprehensibility are part of accessible service design. And it should visibly tell the patient this is a pre-triage tool and a clinician will assess them — managing expectations is part of safe communication.
Alright. We're a B2B buyer, not the manufacturer — give me a procurement-ready checklist of go-live conditions I can put in front of the vendor and my own governance board.

Go-live conditions — AI ED triage chatbot (procurement/governance stub): 1. [P6.D3] Multilingual validation — per-language, per-acuity sensitivity/specificity with CIs and explicit under-triage rates, in your actual populations (not machine-translated proxies). Contractual acceptance criterion; unvalidated languages default to human triage. 2. [P6.D1] Bias — evidence that training data/triage rules don't systematically under-serve specific ethnic/language groups; bias audit and subgroup monitoring post-deployment. 3. [P3.D5] Automation bias — output framed as suggestion + confidence + drivers; nurse must actively assign (no confirm-default); overrides easy, logged, and reviewed; monitor override rate; periodic AI-off audits. 4. [P5.D1] Understandable output — plain-language questions validated with native speakers, reading-level targets, teach-back for critical symptoms; comprehension as a safety control. Accessibility per EAA / EN 301 549. Governance notes: confirm the vendor's EU AI Act classification — ED triage is high-risk AI, pulling in obligations on data quality, human oversight, transparency, and logging — and confirm MDR 2017/745 medical-device status. Make per-language validation, human-oversight design, and post-market monitoring contractual, with a defined fallback to standard triage.

I'm a data scientist at a recovery-support startup. We've trained a model that scores daily relapse risk for people in addiction recovery from phone usage, sleep and check-in data. When the score crosses a threshold we ping the user, and if it's really high we can auto-notify their nominated support contact. Honestly the model's good, AUC 0.83 on holdout, so I think we mostly just need to ship it.

An AUC of 0.83 is a fine signal, but the way you've framed it — "the model's good, so just ship" — is itself one of the bigger risks here. When a counsellor or the user treats a daily number as the truth, you get automation bias [P3.D5]: people stop applying their own judgement and defer to the score, including on a day the model is wrong. With relapse prediction the cost of a false negative (someone reassured by a low score) and a false positive (someone alarmed, or a contact alerted unnecessarily) are both serious, so the score has to be presented as a fallible estimate, not a verdict. Two things I'd want to know before "mostly ship": who acts on the score, and what happens when it's wrong?
Fair. The user sees the score, and the model decides on the auto-alert to the contact. The whole point is it's automatic — that's the product.

Then the auto-alert is the part to slow down on. You're processing health data about a recovering-addiction population, which is special-category data under GDPR Art. 9 and a textbook vulnerable population [P2.D6] — the consequences of a wrongful disclosure (to a partner, a parent, an employer-as-contact) can include shame, relationship damage, even loss of housing or custody. So an automated decision that discloses a sensitive inference to a third party can't just be a threshold firing silently. I'd push for: explicit, separate, revocable consent for the contact-notification feature [P2.D6]; the user choosing exactly who the contact is and what they're told; and ideally a short human-in-the-loop or a user-confirmable hold before the contact is pinged, rather than full automation on the highest-stakes action.
But a hold defeats the purpose — the high-risk moment is exactly when the person won't confirm. That's why we automate it.

That's a legitimate clinical rationale, and it might justify automation — but it's a decision you should make explicitly and document, not one that falls out of "it's the product." The honest framing: automating disclosure trades a missed-alert risk against a wrongful-disclosure-to-a-vulnerable-person risk [P2.D6][P3.D5]. To hold that trade-off responsibly you need to know, per alert, why it fired. Right now can you reconstruct, three weeks later, that user X's contact was notified on the 14th because the score hit 0.91 driven mainly by a sleep-collapse feature, on model version 2.3?
Not cleanly. We log the final score and a timestamp. The feature contributions and model version aren't stored per event.

That's the gap I'd fix first, because it's load-bearing for everything else [P5.D3]. Decision traceability and logging means: for every alert and especially every contact-notification, persist the input snapshot (or a hash), the model version, the score, the threshold in force, the top feature contributions, and the action taken — in an append-only, access-controlled log. That's what lets you (a) investigate a wrongful disclosure when a user complains, (b) explain to a regulator why an automated decision was made, and (c) detect drift when the threshold starts mis-firing. It also feeds the consent story — you can show a user the actual record of when and why their contact was alerted [P2.D6].
Okay. And the third-party part — the contact gets a notification, but also we use Twilio to send the SMS. Does that change anything?

Yes, that's a second sharing surface to nail down [P2.D4]. Twilio (and any analytics or push provider in the path) is a processor handling special-category data, so you need a GDPR Art. 28 data-processing agreement, data minimisation in what you send them (the SMS body should not spell out "high relapse risk" in clear text), and that flow documented in your records of processing. Don't conflate "the support contact" (a recipient the user chose) with "the SMS vendor" (a processor) — they need different legal bases and different disclosures in your consent text [P2.D4][P2.D6].
Got it. Can you give me a short ordered list I can take to the team?

Priority order for this feature: 1. [P5.D3] Per-event traceability log (input snapshot/hash, model version, score, threshold, top feature contributions, action) before any wider rollout — append-only, access-controlled. 2. [P2.D6] Separate, revocable, explicit consent for contact-notification; user picks the contact and what's disclosed; treat the whole feature as special-category processing under GDPR Art. 9. 3. [P3.D5] Reframe the score in-product as a fallible estimate, not a verdict; show drivers; document the automate-vs-human-hold decision for the highest-stakes action rather than defaulting to silent automation. 4. [P2.D4] DPA with Twilio/any processor, minimise message content, no sensitive inference in cleartext SMS; record the flow in your processing register. The model quality is genuinely the easy part — the sensitive-disclosure and "show your work" parts are what make this shippable.

I'm a midwife, advising a small startup. They want pregnant women to take their blood pressure at home with a Bluetooth cuff and an app, mainly to spot pre-eclampsia earlier. The pitch is "fewer clinic visits." I like the idea but something nags at me about telling a pregnant woman she can stay home.

Your instinct is the right one to follow. The core danger of "fewer clinic visits" framed around pre-eclampsia is delayed medical consultation [P1.D4]: pre-eclampsia can escalate fast, and a reassuring-looking home reading — or a borderline one the app doesn't act on — can be the reason a woman waits instead of being seen. The app must never become a substitute for urgent obstetric assessment for red-flag symptoms (severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, reduced fetal movements), regardless of what the cuff says. I'd want the product's safety-netting to be explicit and unmissable, not buried in a disclaimer. Before design specifics — is there a clear escalation pathway defined, or is the plan just to show numbers?
Right now it just shows the systolic/diastolic numbers and a green/amber/red colour. Red says "contact your midwife."

Two problems there. First, a passive "contact your midwife" on a red reading is weak safety-netting for a time-critical condition [P1.D4] — it should specify who to call, when (now, not "soon"), what number, and that symptoms override a "green" reading. Second, the colour bands assume the reading is trustworthy, which brings in measurement reliability [P1.D5]. Consumer Bluetooth cuffs are frequently not validated in pregnancy specifically — many validation studies exclude pregnant women, and pre-eclampsia/cuff-size/arm-position errors can push a genuinely high reading into "amber." Do you know whether the specific cuff is clinically validated for use in pregnancy, not just CE-marked as a general BP device?
Honestly no. They picked the cuff on price and it's CE-marked. I assumed CE meant it was fine for pregnant patients.

That's a common and risky assumption [P1.D5]. CE marking under MDR 2017/745 covers the device's general conformity, not that it's been validated in a pregnant population — those are different things, and pregnancy is exactly where validated accuracy matters because the decision is high-stakes. I'd insist on a cuff with published pregnancy-specific validation (e.g. against a recognised protocol), and the app should reinforce technique: correct cuff size, seated, arm supported, rested, repeat if high. Where readings are estimates from a device not validated in this population, the app should say so rather than implying clinical-grade certainty [P1.D5].
The startup also wants readings to flow automatically into the hospital's maternity record so the team sees trends. That's good, right? Less manual entry for me.

It can be very good — and it's also where reliability and traceability meet [P5.D3][P1.D5]. If readings auto-populate the maternity record, the care team will act on them, so you need to know each entry is trustworthy and reconstructable: which device took it, when, app/firmware version, whether it was a confirmed or single reading, and whether the woman flagged symptoms alongside it. Without that, an out-of-context number in the record can mislead the clinical team as easily as it reassures the patient. Traceability here isn't bureaucracy — it's what lets you trust a remote reading enough to act on it.
How do I make sure the hospital system actually ingests it properly? Their record is some old maternity system.

That's the interoperability question [P4.D2], and "some old system" is the warning sign. Aim for a recognised standard — HL7 FHIR Observation resources for the BP readings, with LOINC codes for systolic/diastolic — rather than a bespoke CSV or screen-scrape that silently breaks on an upgrade. Confirm the maternity system can receive and correctly file those, with units and timestamps preserved and the device/source captured. Test the failure modes: what happens to a reading if the integration is down — does it queue, drop silently, or alert someone? A dropped pre-eclampsia trend is a patient-safety event, not just an IT glitch [P4.D2][P1.D4].
Okay, this is more than the startup thinks. Can you boil it down to what I push back on hardest?

Hardest pushbacks, in order: 1. [P1.D4] Reframe away from "fewer clinic visits." Build explicit safety-netting: symptom red-flags that override any reading, a specific "call now + number" escalation, and clear statements that the app is an adjunct, not a triage replacement. 2. [P1.D5] Use a cuff with pregnancy-specific validation (CE marking alone is not enough under MDR 2017/745); enforce measurement technique; label estimates honestly. 3. [P5.D3] Per-reading traceability into the record: device ID, firmware/app version, timestamp, single-vs-confirmed, symptom flag — so the care team can trust what they act on. 4. [P4.D2] Standards-based integration (HL7 FHIR + LOINC), tested ingestion, and a defined behaviour for when the link fails so no reading is silently lost. Get 1 and 2 right before anyone talks about reducing visits.

I'm an oncology nurse co-designing an app with our IT team. The idea: chemo patients log symptoms between visits — nausea, fever, fatigue, diarrhoea — and we see it on our side so we can call them earlier. We've seen the studies that this improves outcomes, so we're keen. What should we be careful about?

It's a well-evidenced model, so the care is mostly in the failure modes, not the concept. The one that keeps oncology teams up at night is delayed escalation of a dangerous symptom [P1.D4] — above all neutropenic fever, where hours matter. If a patient logs a fever of 38.5°C on a Saturday and the app treats it like any other entry that the team reviews "next working day," you've built a slower path to care, not a faster one. So the first design question is: does the app distinguish symptoms that need immediate action from routine logging, and does it tell the patient to act, not just log?
Right now everything goes into one feed we review during the day. We hadn't separated out the urgent stuff.

That's the highest-priority fix [P1.D4]. You need symptom-severity logic (the validated oncology toolkits like CTCAE-based grading or UKONS-style triage are a good basis) so that a red-flag entry — fever above threshold, uncontrolled vomiting, signs of sepsis — does two things at once: tells the patient immediately and unambiguously to call the acute oncology line or attend, and surfaces to the team through a channel that doesn't depend on someone happening to scroll the feed. The patient-facing instruction matters because the app must reduce the chance they wait, not give them a place to log and feel they've "done something" [P1.D4].
Makes sense. The other thing IT keeps raising is getting this into our hospital systems — bloods, chemo schedule, the EHR. They want to build a custom connector. Is that fine?

Be cautious about "custom connector" [P4.D2]. A bespoke point-to-point integration is exactly what breaks silently on the next EHR upgrade and is hard to maintain or audit. For symptom data and the link to chemo cycle/bloods, push for standards-based exchange — HL7 FHIR resources, SNOMED CT / LOINC coding for the symptoms and observations — so the data is portable and the meaning is preserved across systems. Also define what happens when the connector is down: do urgent symptoms still reach the team by an independent route? Interoperability failures here aren't cosmetic, they can sit directly on the escalation path [P4.D2][P1.D4].
And do we really need heavy logging? It's just symptom entries, and the team's busy.

For a clinical-decision tool, yes — traceability is part of safe care, not overhead [P5.D3]. You need to be able to reconstruct, for any patient: what they reported, exactly when, what severity the app assigned, whether an urgent flag fired, whether it was acknowledged by a clinician and when, and what action followed. That record protects the patient (an unactioned neutropenic-fever flag becomes visible and reviewable), protects the team clinically and medico-legally, and is what lets you audit whether escalations are actually being picked up promptly. Append-only, time-stamped, tied to the patient record [P5.D3].
If that logging shows escalations being missed, that's the kind of thing we'd want to learn from, not just file away.

Exactly — and that's where the logs earn their keep. Two related but distinct things matter here. The traceability log [P5.D3] is your raw material: it lets you go back and review flagged-but-missed escalations and near-misses, feed fixes into the severity thresholds and workflow, and show you do so. Alongside that, be honest with patients about what the app is and isn't [P5.D2] — its limitations should be stated plainly: it supplements the acute oncology line and your team, it does not replace calling when something is wrong, and a quiet feed does not mean "all clear." Communicating those limits is what stops patients over-trusting the app on a bad day.
Good. Lock down the IDs and give me the summary.

Here's the summary with IDs locked down: 1. [P1.D4] Separate urgent symptoms from routine logging; patient-facing "call the acute oncology line now" plus a team channel that doesn't rely on scrolling the feed. 2. [P4.D2] Standards-based exchange (HL7 FHIR, SNOMED CT/LOINC) instead of a fragile custom connector; define the fallback when the link is down. 3. [P5.D3] Append-only, time-stamped traceability: what was reported, severity assigned, flag fired, who acknowledged, what action — tied to the patient record. 4. [P5.D2] State the app's limits to patients plainly (adjunct, not a replacement for calling), and run a regular review of missed/near-miss escalations using the logs. Fix the urgent-vs-routine split first; everything else supports it.

I'm the PM, and I have a legal hat on for this one. We're building an AI mental-health support app aimed at 14-year-olds — mood tracking, a chatbot, some coping exercises. Marketing wants it live across the EU by autumn. From a compliance angle, where do I actually start?

Start from the fact that almost every risk here is amplified because the users are children with mental-health needs — that's vulnerable-population data on two counts at once [P2.D6]. Mental-health data is special-category under GDPR Art. 9, and the data subjects are minors, so the bar for everything (consent, minimisation, design, safeguarding) is higher, and the EU AI Act treats systems exploiting vulnerabilities of children with particular suspicion. "Live across the EU by autumn" is the part I'd challenge first, because consent rules for minors are not uniform across the EU — that alone can break a single autumn launch. So the starting point is: who can lawfully consent for a 14-year-old, and that answer changes by country.
Wait — I assumed if a 14-year-old can sign up to most apps, ours is fine too. Isn't 13 the standard?

That's the common misconception, and it's worth getting exact [P3.D4][P7.D4]. Under GDPR Art. 8 the digital age of consent for information-society services is 16 by default. Member States may lower it, and they have — France set it at 15, Spain at 14, Belgium at 13 — so there is no single EU number. For a 14-year-old: in Spain they may consent themselves; in France (15) and in the 16 default countries they cannot, so you need verifiable parental consent. A pan-EU launch therefore needs per-country consent logic, not one flow. And note "13 is standard" is a US/COPPA reflex, not EU law.
Ugh. Okay, so in the countries where the 14-year-old can't consent alone, the parent consents. That's just one extra checkbox, surely?

It's more than a checkbox, and this is where dynamic consent and withdrawal rights matter [P3.D4]. First, parental consent has to be verifiable, not a self-declared "I am my parent" tickbox — Art. 8 requires reasonable efforts to verify. Second, you now have two parties with rights over one account: the child and the parent, and they can diverge. The child can withdraw consent and must be able to (withdrawal has to be as easy as giving it under Art. 7), and you have to decide what happens to a distressed teenager's data and access if a parent withdraws on their behalf. Third, when the minor reaches the digital-consent age, consent given by the parent should be revisited. For a mental-health app, a parent yanking access or seeing a child's mood logs is also a safeguarding and trust issue, not only a legal one [P3.D4][P2.D6].
This is getting heavy. Is there one formal thing the lawyers will ask me for that I should get ahead of?

Yes — a Data Protection Impact Assessment [P7.D4]. Under GDPR Art. 35 a DPIA is effectively mandatory here: you're doing large-scale processing of special-category data (mental health) about vulnerable data subjects (children), with an AI/chatbot component — that hits multiple Art. 35 triggers and the regulators' own lists. Get your DPO involved now, not after build. The DPIA should document the lawful basis and per-country consent model, data minimisation (does mood-tracking really need everything you're collecting from a child?), the chatbot's risks, retention, and your mitigations. Doing it early actually de-risks the autumn date because it forces the consent and data decisions before they're baked into code.
And the AI chatbot specifically — does the minor angle change how we handle consent and data for that?

It does, and it ties back to consent and vulnerable data together [P2.D1][P2.D6]. The consent and the privacy information have to be genuinely understandable to a 14-year-old, not adult legalese — informed consent for a minor means age-appropriate, plain-language explanation of what the chatbot does, what's recorded, who can see it (including the parent), and crucially that it is not a clinician or a crisis service [P2.D1]. For special-category minors' data you want strict minimisation and clear limits on using their conversations to train models [P2.D6]. The chatbot also needs a safe-handling path for disclosures of self-harm or abuse — but flag that as its own clinical-safety workstream; here I'm scoping the consent and data side.
Alright. Give me the compliance starting list to take to legal and the DPO.

Compliance starter, prioritised: 1. [P7.D4] Run a DPIA now (GDPR Art. 35) with the DPO — mental-health + minors + AI is a clear mandatory case; let it drive the consent and data design before build. 2. [P3.D4] Per-country digital-consent logic: GDPR Art. 8 default 16, France 15, Spain 14, Belgium 13. For a 14-year-old this means self-consent in Spain, verifiable parental consent elsewhere. Build verifiable parental consent, easy child-initiated withdrawal (Art. 7), a dual child/parent rights model, and a re-consent step at the age threshold. 3. [P2.D6] Treat all of it as special-category data on vulnerable minors (Art. 9): strict minimisation, tight retention, explicit limits on training the chatbot on their conversations. 4. [P2.D1] Age-appropriate, plain-language consent and privacy notices a 14-year-old can actually understand, stating the app is not a clinician or crisis service. The single thing that most threatens your autumn date is the per-country consent model — resolve that and the DPIA first.
